Verizon Device Financing: EDA¶

Name: Obaro Erigha
Term: Autumn 2026

Data: 300,000 simulated applications, 1 Jan 2023 to 31 Dec 2024. Each answer is followed by the code and output behind it.

Executive summary¶

  • Verizon changed its approval rules twice: looser on 1 Aug 2023 (promotion) and tighter on 1 May 2024. Both changes came from the score and its cut-offs. The applicants themselves did not change.
  • On 1 May 2024, defaults rose about 55% for applicants with the same profile. Customers started repaying worse. The tightening did not cause this; it slightly reduced it.
  • The internal risk score (IRS) ranks risk better than credit score alone (holdout AUC 0.590 vs 0.563). A simple logistic model (credit score, income, two age steps, existing customer, regime) does better again (AUC 0.620) and is well calibrated.
  • Verizon is far too cautious for its own economics. A plan earns +25% of device price if repaid and loses 35% if it defaults, so it breaks even at a 41.7% default probability. The riskiest tenth of funded plans in the final regime defaults at only 17%.
  • Counteroffers lose money. A larger down payment or a cheaper device does not lower default, but 35–50% of customers who get one walk away.
  • Recommendation: approve more, in steps. (1) Approve conditional applicants on the terms they asked for (about +$1.0M). (2) Move the deny cut-off back to the 2023–24 level, where real outcome data exist (+$0.25M to +$1.1M). (3) Test a random sample above that level. Steps 1 and 2 add about $2.1M (+18%) to the final regime's $12.0M profit.

0. Data and definitions¶

Files: FEED Data/Verizon Data.csv (300,000 rows × 18 columns) and FEED Data/Verizon data dictionary.xlsx.

Column Type Notes
application_date date 727 days. No applications on Thanksgiving or Christmas in either year
race, hisp, gender text Self-reported, includes "PreferNot". Used only for fairness checks, not as predictors
age int 18–79
income float $15,000–$200,000. Spikes at the floor (2,116 rows) and the cap (2,229), so values are likely capped there
credit_score int 327–850
existing_customer 0/1 40% are existing customers
device_requested / device_final text Low / Mid / High
device_price int $379–$1,219 (five prices per tier)
down_payment_base / final float Share of device price. down_payment_base = 0.205 − 0.00015 × credit_score exactly (R² = 1), so it adds nothing beyond credit score
internal_risk_score float Mean 0, SD 1; higher = riskier. Observed range −4.06 to 4.36 (the dictionary says −3.74 to 6.87)
initial_decision / final_status text See below
default_flag float The only column with missing values (34,940)
profit float 0 for plans that were not funded

How the decisions fit together

initial_decision Funded_Original Funded_Revised Not_Funded
Approve 242,673 0 0
Conditional (counteroffer) 0 22,387 16,706
Deny 0 0 18,234
  • Funded = Funded_Original + Funded_Revised (265,060 plans). Only these have a default_flag. Overall default rate: 8.03%.
  • Not funded = Not_Funded (34,940): denied applicants plus conditional applicants who turned down the counteroffer. No default_flag, profit 0.
  • Profit is a fixed share of price: exactly +0.25 × price if repaid and −0.35 × price if defaulted, in every row and regime. The down payment does not affect it.

Regimes (dates found in Q4a; used throughout):

Regime Dates Applications Approve rate Funded rate Default rate (funded)
R1: baseline 2023-01-01 to 2023-07-31 87,469 81.5% 88.7% 6.95%
R2: promotion (looser) 2023-08-01 to 2024-04-30 112,251 88.9% 93.8% 6.75%
R3: tightened 2024-05-01 to 2024-12-31 100,280 71.4% 81.9% 10.69%

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Load and inspect
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
section("0. DATA INSPECTION")
dd = pd.read_excel(DICT)
print(dd.to_string())
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, parse_dates=["application_date"])
print("shape", df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print("missing:\n", df.isna().sum()[df.isna().sum() > 0])
print(pd.crosstab(df.initial_decision, df.final_status, margins=True))
print("missing days:", pd.date_range("2023-01-01", "2024-12-31").difference(df.application_date.unique()).date)

df["regime"] = np.select([df.application_date < BREAK1, df.application_date < BREAK2], ["R1", "R2"], "R3")
df["funded"] = (df.final_status != "Not_Funded").astype(int)
df["approve"] = (df.initial_decision == "Approve").astype(int)
df["log_inc"] = np.log(df.income)
df["downgrade"] = (df.device_requested != df.device_final).astype(int)
df["dp_increase"] = df.down_payment_final - df.down_payment_base
df["year"] = df.application_date.dt.year
df["month"] = df.application_date.dt.month
f = df[df.funded == 1].copy()          # funded = Funded_Original + Funded_Revised (default_flag observed)
nf = df[df.funded == 0].copy()         # not funded = default_flag missing

print(df.groupby("regime").agg(start=("application_date", "min"), end=("application_date", "max"),
                               n=("age", "size"), approve=("approve", "mean"), funded=("funded", "mean")))

# profit structure (needed in Q7/Q8)
f["margin"] = f.profit / f.device_price
print(f.groupby("default_flag").margin.agg(["min", "max", "mean"]))
f["cs_band"] = pd.cut(f.credit_score, [0, 550, 600, 650, 700, 900])   # used in Q2 and Q4e

Regime dates (Q4a, computed first)¶

Every question uses the regimes, so the break dates are found here first. The written Q4a answer is in the Q4 section.

In [18]:
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4a. Structural breaks (computed first; everything else uses the regimes)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
section("Q4a. STRUCTURAL BREAKS")
daily = df.groupby("application_date").agg(n=("age", "size"), irs=("internal_risk_score", "mean"),
                                            approve=("approve", "mean"),
                                            deny=("initial_decision", lambda s: (s == "Deny").mean()),
                                            default=("default_flag", "mean"), cs=("credit_score", "mean"))
# residual score: IRS minus what applicant characteristics predict (fit on R1 only)
irs_fit = smf.ols("internal_risk_score ~ credit_score + log_inc + age + existing_customer + C(device_requested)",
                  df[df.regime == "R1"]).fit()
df["irs_resid"] = df.internal_risk_score - irs_fit.predict(df)
daily["irs_resid"] = df.groupby("application_date").irs_resid.mean()
for b in [BREAK1, BREAK2]:
    print(daily.loc[b - pd.Timedelta(days=6): b + pd.Timedelta(days=5)].round(3).to_string())

# search: the single day that maximises the before/after difference in the daily residual score
def best_split(series, lo, hi):
    out = {}
    for d in series.loc[lo:hi].index:
        out[d] = abs(series.loc[d:d + pd.Timedelta(days=30)].mean() - series.loc[d - pd.Timedelta(days=30):d - pd.Timedelta(days=1)].mean())
    return max(out, key=out.get), max(out.values())
print("best split 2023:", best_split(daily.irs_resid, "2023-03-01", "2023-12-01"))
print("best split 2024:", best_split(daily.irs_resid, "2024-02-01", "2024-11-30"))

print("decision thresholds by regime (min/max IRS per initial_decision):")
print(df.groupby(["regime", "initial_decision"]).internal_risk_score.agg(["min", "max", "count"]).round(3))
for r, g in df.groupby("regime"):
    m = smf.ols("internal_risk_score ~ credit_score + log_inc + age + existing_customer + C(device_requested)", g).fit()
    print(r, m.params.round(4).to_dict(), "R2=", round(m.rsquared, 3))

wk = df.set_index("application_date").resample("W")
weekly = pd.DataFrame({"irs": wk.internal_risk_score.mean(), "approve": wk.approve.mean(),
                       "default": wk.default_flag.mean(), "cs": wk.credit_score.mean()})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True)
for a, col, lab in zip(ax, ["irs", "approve", "default"],
                       ["Mean internal risk score", "Initial approval rate", "Default rate (funded)"]):

Q1. Age¶

Q1a. Which ages are over-represented?¶

Ages 18, 21, 25, 30, 40 and 65 have far more applicants than their neighbours, and 79 looks like a top-code. This is not realistic. Real age counts change smoothly from year to year. Spikes at round or milestone ages point to rounding, estimated ages or form defaults. The spike at 18 is most likely a floor value (minimum age or a default entry).

Age Count Average of the two neighbouring ages Ratio
18 14,425 (19: 2,561) 5.6× age 19
21 8,130 3,369 2.4×
25 10,899 5,148 2.1×
30 13,340 7,366 1.8×
40 14,021 9,008 1.6×
65 3,150 755 4.2×
79 84 (78: 30) 2.8× age 78, likely a top-code

The ages next to each spike are short of people (19 and 20 are under 0.6× their neighbours; 64 and 66 are 0.44× and 0.33×). So true ages are being moved onto the round number. People in each spike have similar credit scores and incomes to the neighbouring ages, so they really are people near that age.

Q1b. Does default risk change smoothly with age?¶

No. It changes in steps at 25 and 67, and is almost flat in between.

Age band Funded plans Default rate
18–24 29,755 11.9% (each year from 18 to 24 is 11.6–12.4%)
25–66 232,978 7.5% (8.3% at 25, easing to about 7% in the 60s)
67+ 2,327 9.4%

The steps are sharp: 11.9% at 24 vs 8.3% at 25, and 7.0% at 65, 8.0% at 66, 10.2% at 67. Two step dummies fit better than a quadratic in age with the same number of parameters (log-likelihood −73,750 vs −73,775). The steps stay significant after controlling for credit score and income (age < 25: +0.36 log-odds; age ≥ 67: +0.38).

Q1c. Why smooth vs bucketed age matters more here¶

The risk steps fall exactly where applicants pile up.

  1. The true risk curve is a step. A smooth fit spreads the 3.6-point drop at 25 over many years. A quadratic predicts 10.8% at 21 (actual 12.0%), 9.6% at 25 (actual 8.3%) and 8.0% at 67 (actual 10.2%). It underprices the young and the over-67s and overprices people in their late 20s.
  2. The biggest spikes sit on or next to the steps. Age 25 has 10,899 applicants (3.6% of all), more than any other age under 30, and 65 is a 4× spike just below the upper step. Where the boundary goes changes thousands of predictions at once: a cut at "< 25" gives the young bucket 11.9%; a cut at "≤ 25" pulls in the 25-year-olds and drops it to 11.1%. One year moves about 11,000 predictions by about 4 points.
  3. Ages near the steps are the least reliable. The spikes show rounding or misreporting, and a hard cut-off rewards it: saying "25" instead of "24" cuts predicted risk by a third. If Verizon uses age steps, it should verify date of birth near the cut-offs.

# Q1 Age
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
section("Q1. AGE")
a = df.groupby("age").size().rename("n").to_frame()
a["neighbor_avg"] = (a.n.shift(1) + a.n.shift(-1)) / 2
a["ratio"] = a.n / a.neighbor_avg
a["n_funded"] = f.groupby("age").size()
a["default"] = f.groupby("age").default_flag.mean()
a["credit"] = df.groupby("age").credit_score.mean()
print(a.round(3).to_string())
print("heaped ages (ratio > 1.4 or endpoints):", a[(a.ratio > 1.4)].index.tolist())
f["age_band"] = pd.cut(f.age, [17, 24, 66, 80], labels=["18-24", "25-66", "67+"])
print(f.groupby("age_band", observed=True).default_flag.agg(["mean", "size"]).round(4))
# step test: logistic with steps vs. smooth quadratic
f["age_lt25"] = (f.age < 25).astype(int); f["age_ge67"] = (f.age >= 67).astype(int)
for fm in ["default_flag ~ age + I(age**2)", "default_flag ~ age_lt25 + age_ge67",
           "default_flag ~ age + I(age**2) + age_lt25 + age_ge67",
           "default_flag ~ credit_score + log_inc + age + I(age**2)",
           "default_flag ~ credit_score + log_inc + age + I(age**2) + age_lt25 + age_ge67"]:
    m = smf.logit(fm, f).fit(disp=0)
    print(f"{fm:80s} LL={m.llf:.1f} AIC={m.aic:.1f}", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in m.params.items() if "age" in k})
for lo, hi in [(22, 27), (63, 70)]:
    g = f[f.age.between(lo, hi)]
    print(g.groupby("age").default_flag.agg(["mean", "size"]).round(4).T)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7), sharex=True)

Q2. Income¶

Q2a. Do risk scores, approvals and defaults differ by income?¶

Yes. The IRS and approval rate change a lot with income (both U-shaped); default changes much less. Default falls with income up to about $85k, is flat to about $130k, and rises again at the top.

Income n Mean IRS Approve rate Default rate (funded)
$15–25k 20,180 +1.10 40% 10.1%
$25–35k 38,378 +0.66 61% 9.7%
$35–45k 46,351 +0.31 75% 8.7%
$45–55k 44,215 +0.03 84% 8.3%
$55–65k 37,274 −0.23 91% 7.5%
$65–75k 29,289 −0.42 94% 7.2%
$75–85k 22,226 −0.56 96% 6.9%
$85–100k 22,809 −0.67 97% 7.0%
$100–115k 14,632 −0.71 97% 6.8%
$115–130k 9,067 −0.65 96% 6.8%
$130–145k 5,614 −0.46 94% 7.8%
$145–160k 3,416 −0.17 89% 8.2%
$160–175k 2,217 +0.21 78% 8.1%
$175–200k 4,332 +1.16 38% 11.4%
  • IRS: falls about 1.8 SD from the lowest incomes to $100–115k, then rises 1.9 SD to the top bin. Even after controlling for credit score, age and existing customer, the score adds a large penalty above about $115k (+2.2 SD in the top bin).
  • Approval: tracks the IRS: 40% → 97% → 38%. The top earners are approved about as rarely as the bottom.
  • Default: a much flatter U: 10.1% at the bottom, 6.8% in the middle, 11.4% in the top bin (among the 68% of top earners who were funded). Some upturn at high income is real, but approvals swing far more than risk does.

Q2b. Does income add information beyond credit score? Beyond the IRS?¶

Beyond credit score: yes, clearly. Beyond the IRS: statistically yes, but negligible in practice.

Likelihood-ratio tests on the 265,060 funded plans:

Base model + income term LR χ² df p
credit_score log income 200.8 1 1e-45
credit_score spline(log income) 465.6 4 2e-99
IRS + regime log income 7.2 1 0.007
IRS + regime spline(log income) 25.1 4 5e-5

The cross-tabs agree. Within a credit-score band, default still falls with income (550–600 band: 11.4% in the lowest income quintile vs 7.1% in the fourth). Within an IRS quintile (per regime), default barely moves with income (top IRS quintile: 12.6%, 12.7%, 12.1%, 11.6%, 12.8%). The IRS already uses income, as Verizon says.

# Q2b: does income add information beyond credit score / beyond IRS? (likelihood-ratio tests, funded plans)
f["log_inc"] = np.log(f.income)
def lr_test(base, full, data):
    m0 = smf.logit(base, data).fit(disp=0); m1 = smf.logit(full, data).fit(disp=0)
    lr = 2 * (m1.llf - m0.llf); k = len(m1.params) - len(m0.params)
    return round(lr, 1), k, stats.chi2.sf(lr, k), m1

Q3. Default flag¶

Q3a. Who has no default_flag?¶

Exactly the 34,940 applicants who were not funded. Every funded plan has the flag.

initial_decision default_flag missing observed
Approve 0 242,673
Conditional 16,706 (turned down the counteroffer) 22,387 (accepted it)
Deny 18,234 (all of them) 0

Q3b. Final regime: share of not-funded applicants riskier than every funded one¶

61.7% (11,195 of 18,131). The highest IRS among R3 funded plans is 1.502, the R3 deny cut-off. Every R3 denial (IRS 1.502 to 4.358) is above it. Every R3 applicant who turned down a counteroffer (IRS 0.845 to 1.502) is inside the funded range.

Q3c. Can a model trained on funded plans be trusted for denied applicants?¶

For denied applicants, not much. For those who turned down a counteroffer, reasonably. And for most R3 denials, the looser R2 regime provides real outcome data.

  • Denied applicants: low trust. All R3 denials lie outside the score range the model learned from, so any estimate is extrapolation and depends on the chosen functional form. For example, a logistic fit on R3 funded plans already under-predicts the riskiest funded decile (15% fitted vs 17% actual). Denied applicants may also differ in ways the data don't record, and none of it can be checked.
  • Applicants who turned down a counteroffer: more trust. They look like those who accepted (mean IRS 1.23 vs 1.16, credit score 547 vs 547), and those who accepted have outcomes. The differences are mostly observable (lower income, $38k vs $58k; fewer existing customers, 24% vs 34%), so a model can adjust for them. Some hidden self-selection may remain.
  • R3 denials that R2 would have funded: also more trust. The same applicant scores 0.53 higher in R3 than in R2, and R2 funded up to 1.92. After removing each regime's score offset (Q4a), 86.6% of R3 denials (9,699) fall inside the range R2 actually funded. R2 outcomes for these people, scaled up for the R3 shock, are evidence rather than extrapolation. This assumes the shock raises their default by about the same proportion as everyone else's; Q4e shows it does (about 1.5–2.1×).

Q4. Structural breaks¶

Q4a. Break dates¶

Break 1: 1 August 2023. Break 2: 1 May 2024.

Method: take the IRS minus what applicant characteristics predict (credit score, log income, age, existing customer, device; fitted on R1). Searching every day for the largest 30-day before/after jump picks out exactly these two dates.

Day Mean IRS residual Approve Deny Default
2023-07-31 +0.02 82.9% 6.6% 7.6%
2023-08-01 −0.22 91.2% 1.3% 6.3%
2024-04-30 −0.25 90.3% 1.1% 6.6%
2024-05-01 +0.31 70.6% 13.6% 10.7%

The decision cut-offs, read from the data, change on the same days:

Regime Approve if IRS ≤ Conditional Deny if IRS > Score offset for the same applicant (vs R1)
R1 0.845 0.845–1.502 1.502 0
R2 0.960 0.960–1.922 1.922 −0.24
R3 0.845 0.845–1.502 1.502 +0.29

The score's weights on credit score (−0.0115), log income (−0.61) and existing customer (−0.38) are identical in all three regimes. Only the intercept moves.

Code and output for Q4a are in the Regime dates section near the top.

Q4b. Which columns shift, and when?¶

Comparison of 60 days before vs 60 days after each break (Welch t-test for numeric columns, χ² for categorical).

Column Break 1 (Aug 2023) Break 2 (May 2024) Shifts at
credit_score 609.4 → 609.3 (p = 0.79) 608.9 → 609.2 (p = 0.57) Neither
age 37.8 → 37.8 (p = 0.91) 37.8 → 37.7 (p = 0.54) Neither

existing_customer 40.6% → 39.5% (p = 0.01*) 40.2% → 39.6% (p = 0.19) Neither (*regime means are 39.9%, 40.0%, 40.0%)
device_requested p = 0.15 p = 0.36 Neither

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4b. Which columns shift at which break (60-day windows either side; Welch t / chi-square)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
section("Q4b. SHIFTS AT EACH BREAK")
cols = ["credit_score", "age", "income", "existing_customer", "device_requested", "internal_risk_score",
        "initial_decision", "default_flag"]
rows = []
for name, b in [("Break1", BREAK1), ("Break2", BREAK2)]:
    pre = df[(df.application_date >= b - pd.Timedelta(days=60)) & (df.application_date < b)]
    post = df[(df.application_date >= b) & (df.application_date < b + pd.Timedelta(days=60))]
    for c in cols:
        if df[c].dtype == object or str(df[c].dtype) in ("str", "string"):
            tab = pd.crosstab(pd.concat([pre, post])[c], np.r_[np.zeros(len(pre)), np.ones(len(post))])
            p = stats.chi2_contingency(tab)[1]
            pre_v = pre[c].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3).to_dict()
            post_v = post[c].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3).to_dict()
        else:
            a, bb = pre[c].dropna(), post[c].dropna()
            p = stats.ttest_ind(a, bb, equal_var=False).pvalue
            pre_v, post_v = round(a.mean(), 4), round(bb.mean(), 4)
        rows.append(dict(brk=name, col=c, pre=pre_v, post=post_v, p=p))
shift = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(shift.to_string())
print(df.groupby("regime")[["credit_score", "age", "income", "existing_customer", "internal_risk_score",
                            "irs_resid", "approve", "default_flag"]].mean().round(4))
print(pd.crosstab(df.regime, df.initial_decision, normalize="index").round(3))
print(pd.crosstab(df.regime, df.device_requested, normalize="index").round(3))

Q4c. What the pattern means¶

At break 1, only Verizon's scoring and cut-offs changed (the score fell 0.24 for the same applicant and the cut-offs loosened). Applicants and repayment stayed the same, so this was a purely internal promotional loosening. At break 2, the score was tightened (+0.53), the applicants still didn't change, yet defaults jumped about 55%. That points to an outside economic shock to repayment, with Verizon tightening in response.

Q4d. Are defaults seasonal?¶

No, I disagree with the teammate. The "May jump" is the 1 May 2024 regime change, which pooling months across years mixes in.

Months 2023 2024 Pooled (teammate's view)
Jan–Apr (average) 6.96% 6.65% 6.80%
May–Dec (average) 6.86% 10.69% 8.66%
  • In 2023, May–December is not higher than January–April (6.9% vs 7.0%). Every 2023 month is 6.6–7.2%.
  • In 2024, the jump happens exactly on 1 May and then stays flat (10.2–11.2% each month). That is the R3 shock, not a season.
  • Within each regime, month does not predict default (χ² p = 0.53, 0.62, 0.41 for R1, R2, R3). Month dummies add nothing once regime is included (LR χ² = 7.4, df = 11, p = 0.77).
  • The one real seasonal pattern is in the applicants: average credit score drops about 10 points in November and December both years (609 → 599). Holiday defaults are still not higher.

Tightening every summer and fall would cut profitable volume to fix a pattern that isn't there.

Q4e. Did the tightening backfire?¶

No, I disagree with the teammate. Defaults rose 3–4 points in every risk band, so the economy drove the rise. The tightening slightly lowered the funded default rate.

Default rate by IRS quintile (same cut-points for all regimes, funded plans):

IRS quintile R1 R2 R3
Q1 (safest) 5.6% 5.6% 8.8%
Q2 5.2% 5.4% 8.4%
Q3 5.5% 5.4% 8.9%
Q4 7.3% 7.2% 10.2%
Q5 (riskiest) 11.5% 11.7% 14.9%
  • R3 defaults are 3–4 points higher in every band. The same holds on a score that stays fixed across regimes (characteristics only) and within credit-score bands (e.g. 700+: 5.1% in R2 vs 8.2% in R3). The shock hits everyone; it is not a change in who got funded.
  • Because the R3 score is shifted up, an R3 applicant in a given band is actually safer than an R1/R2 applicant in that band. So the table understates the shock.
  • Counterfactual: with R2's funded risk mix and R3's within-band default rates, R3 would have defaulted at 11.2%, not 10.7%. Tightening cut defaults by about 0.5 points.
  • The fair criticism of the tightening is about profit, not defaults. The applicants it removed would default at about 16–25% (Q8), well under the 41.7% break-even, so it turned away profitable business.

Q5. Internal risk score vs a naive credit-score model¶

The IRS is better overall (holdout AUC 0.590 vs 0.563; 95% CI of the difference [0.022, 0.032]). No subgroup shows the credit-score model meaningfully better.

Setup: logistic regressions on funded plans, 70/30 train/holdout split stratified by regime and default (185,542 / 79,518), all metrics on the holdout.

Model AUC Log-loss Brier
credit_score only 0.563 0.2777 0.0735
internal_risk_score only 0.590 0.2760 0.0732

Metric: AUC. Approval works by ranking applicants and cutting the list at a threshold. AUC measures exactly that: the chance a random defaulter is ranked riskier than a random non-defaulter. It doesn't depend on where the cut-off is set, and it isn't distorted by R3's higher base rate the way accuracy would be. Because the break-even decision in Q8 needs probabilities, log-loss and Brier score are reported too as calibration checks.

Subgroups (holdout AUC):

Subgroup Credit score IRS Comment
R1 / R2 / R3 0.573 / 0.573 / 0.557 0.585 / 0.583 / 0.572 IRS better in every regime
New / existing customers 0.568 / 0.554 0.613 / 0.576 IRS better
Credit score ≤ 550 0.536 0.595 IRS much better
Credit score > 650 0.495–0.497 0.514–0.526 Both close to random
Income $100–130k 0.545 0.537 Only place credit score is ahead, but the CI of the difference is [−0.020, +0.004]: a tie
Income ≥ $130k 0.547 0.592 IRS better: it captures the high-income upturn

Two weaknesses of the IRS:

  • Fitted on all regimes together, both single-score models under-predict R3: 8.6% (IRS) and 7.9% (credit score) vs 10.7% actual, because neither knows about the shock.
  • In R3, the six lowest IRS deciles all default at 8.2–9.4%. The IRS can't tell lower-risk applicants apart.
In [25]:
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q5 / Q6 Models (funded plans, 70/30 stratified holdout)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
section("Q5. CREDIT SCORE vs INTERNAL RISK SCORE")
train, test = train_test_split(f, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=f.regime + f.default_flag.astype(str))
train, test = train.copy(), test.copy()
print("train", train.shape, "test", test.shape, "test default rate", test.default_flag.mean().round(4))

def evaluate(name, p, data=test):
    return dict(model=name, AUC=roc_auc_score(data.default_flag, p), logloss=log_loss(data.default_flag, p),
                Brier=brier_score_loss(data.default_flag, p))

m_cs = smf.logit("default_flag ~ credit_score", train).fit(disp=0)
m_irs = smf.logit("default_flag ~ internal_risk_score", train).fit(disp=0)
test["p_cs"] = m_cs.predict(test); test["p_irs"] = m_irs.predict(test)
res = [evaluate("credit_score only", test.p_cs), evaluate("internal_risk_score only", test.p_irs)]
print(pd.DataFrame(res).round(4))

def sub_auc(data, by):
    out = []
    for k, g in data.groupby(by, observed=True):
        if g.default_flag.nunique() < 2:
            continue
        out.append(dict(group=f"{by}={k}", n=len(g), dflt=g.default_flag.mean(),
                        AUC_cs=roc_auc_score(g.default_flag, g.p_cs), AUC_irs=roc_auc_score(g.default_flag, g.p_irs)))
    return out
test["age_band"] = pd.cut(test.age, [17, 24, 66, 80], labels=["18-24", "25-66", "67+"])
test["inc_band"] = pd.cut(test.income, [0, 35000, 60000, 100000, 130000, 300000])
test["cs_band"] = pd.cut(test.credit_score, [0, 550, 600, 650, 700, 900])
rows = []
for by in ["regime", "existing_customer", "final_status", "device_final", "age_band", "inc_band", "cs_band"]:
    rows += sub_auc(test, by)
sub = pd.DataFrame(rows); sub["irs_minus_cs"] = sub.AUC_irs - sub.AUC_cs
print(sub.round(4).to_string())
# bootstrap CI for high-income subgroup difference
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for lab, g in [("income 100-130k", test[(test.income > 100000) & (test.income <= 130000)]), ("credit>650", test[test.credit_score > 650]), ("income>=130k", test[test.income >= 130000]), ("all", test)]:
    diffs = []
    for _ in range(300):
        s = g.sample(len(g), replace=True, random_state=rng.integers(1e9))
        diffs.append(roc_auc_score(s.default_flag, s.p_irs) - roc_auc_score(s.default_flag, s.p_cs))
    print(lab, "AUC(irs)-AUC(cs) 95% CI:", np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5]).round(4))
# calibration of IRS-only model in R3
print("mean predicted vs actual by regime (IRS model):")
print(test.groupby("regime")[["p_irs", "p_cs", "default_flag"]].mean().round(4))

Q6. A better default model¶

A logistic model with credit-score and income splines, two age steps, existing customer and regime dummies reaches a holdout AUC of 0.620. That is about +0.03 over the IRS and +0.06 over credit score, with bootstrap CIs that exclude zero, and it is well calibrated.

Model (same holdout) AUC Log-loss Brier
credit_score only 0.563 0.2777 0.0735
IRS only 0.590 0.2760 0.0732
IRS + regime dummies 0.603 0.2747 0.0730
Linear logit on raw features 0.605 0.2745 0.0730
New model: spline/step logistic 0.620 0.2728 0.0728
New model + IRS 0.621 0.2726 0.0727
Gradient boosting, same raw inputs 0.621 0.2726 0.0728

Bootstrap 95% CIs of the new model's AUC gain: vs credit score [0.050, 0.064]; vs IRS [0.024, 0.038]; vs IRS + regime [0.013, 0.021].

Model:

logit P(default) = β₀ + s₁(credit_score) + s₂(log income) + β₁·1[age < 25] + β₂·1[age ≥ 67] + β₃·existing_customer + β₄·R2 + β₅·R3

s₁ and s₂ are B-splines with 5 degrees of freedom.

Term Coefficient (log-odds) Odds ratio Why it's there
age < 25 +0.356 1.43 Step from Q1. Replaces linear age, which is about 0 once the steps are in
age ≥ 67 +0.391 1.48 Step from Q1
existing_customer +0.202 1.22 Existing customers default more, yet the IRS gives them a bonus
R3 +0.502 1.65 Final-regime shock (Q4); use R3 for scoring today
R2 −0.083 0.92
spline(log income) U-shape Default falls with income, then rises above about $130k (Q2)
spline(credit_score) Falls, then flat above about 650 Credit score stops helping above about 650

Tried and dropped:

  • down_payment_base: an exact function of credit score.
  • down_payment_final and downgrade: results of the negotiation, and they don't predict default once risk is controlled for (Q7).
  • Device tier: not significant.
  • Gradient boosting: matches but doesn't beat the logistic model, so the engineered terms capture the structure.
  • Adding the IRS: only +0.001. The IRS knows nothing these inputs don't.

Calibration. Average predicted default by regime: 6.93% / 6.73% / 10.67% vs actual 6.95% / 6.75% / 10.68%. By predicted decile: 4.3% to 15.0% predicted vs 4.5% to 14.8% actual.

Caveat. Within R3 alone the gain over the IRS is smaller (AUC 0.578 vs 0.572). A model fitted only on R3 reaches 0.579, so ranking is simply harder in the shock regime. The pooled gain comes partly from the steps and splines (R1/R2: about +0.02 to +0.03) and partly from the regime adjustment.

Why the metric matters for Verizon. Verizon must sort applicants into approve, counteroffer and deny at in-store speed, and AUC measures how well that sorting works. The 41.7% break-even (Q8) also makes it a question of probabilities, so calibration (log-loss) matters: a well-ranked but mis-calibrated score puts the cut-off in the wrong place. Both single-score models under-predict R3 by 2–3 points. The new model does better on both.

In [26]:
section("Q6. IMPROVED MODEL")
# down_payment_base is an exact linear function of credit score (checked here), so it adds nothing
chk = smf.ols("down_payment_base ~ credit_score", df).fit()
print("down_payment_base = %.4f %+.6f*credit_score, R2=%.6f" % (chk.params.iloc[0], chk.params.iloc[1], chk.rsquared))

def add_features(d):
    d = d.copy()
    d["age_lt25"] = (d.age < 25).astype(int)
    d["age_ge67"] = (d.age >= 67).astype(int)
    d["R3"] = (d.regime == "R3").astype(int)
    d["R2"] = (d.regime == "R2").astype(int)
    return d
train, test = add_features(train), add_features(test)
CS = "bs(credit_score, df=5, lower_bound=300, upper_bound=851)"
LI = "bs(log_inc, df=5, lower_bound=9.6, upper_bound=12.3)"
form_logit = f"default_flag ~ {CS} + {LI} + age_lt25 + age_ge67 + existing_customer + R2 + R3"
m_new = smf.logit(form_logit, train).fit(disp=0, maxiter=200)
test["p_new"] = m_new.predict(test)
m_new2 = smf.logit(form_logit + " + internal_risk_score", train).fit(disp=0, maxiter=200)
test["p_new2"] = m_new2.predict(test)
m_lin = smf.logit("default_flag ~ credit_score + log_inc + age + existing_customer + R2 + R3", train).fit(disp=0)
test["p_lin"] = m_lin.predict(test)
m_irs_reg = smf.logit("default_flag ~ internal_risk_score + R2 + R3", train).fit(disp=0)
test["p_irs_reg"] = m_irs_reg.predict(test)
feats = ["credit_score", "income", "age", "existing_customer", "R2", "R3"]
gbm = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=400, learning_rate=0.05, max_leaf_nodes=15, min_samples_leaf=200,
                                     l2_regularization=1.0, random_state=0, early_stopping=True,
                                     validation_fraction=0.15)
gbm.fit(train[feats], train.default_flag)
test["p_gbm"] = gbm.predict_proba(test[feats])[:, 1]
res6 = res + [evaluate("IRS + regime dummies", test.p_irs_reg),
              evaluate("Linear logit, raw features (no engineering)", test.p_lin),
              evaluate("NEW: spline/step logistic", test.p_new),
              evaluate("NEW + IRS", test.p_new2),
              evaluate("Gradient boosting (same raw features)", test.p_gbm)]
res6 = pd.DataFrame(res6); print(res6.round(4).to_string())
print(m_new.summary2().tables[1].round(4).to_string())
for lab, col in [("cs", "p_cs"), ("irs", "p_irs"), ("irs_reg", "p_irs_reg")]:
    diffs = []
    for _ in range(300):
        s = test.sample(len(test), replace=True, random_state=rng.integers(1e9))
        diffs.append(roc_auc_score(s.default_flag, s.p_new) - roc_auc_score(s.default_flag, s[col]))
    print(f"AUC(new)-AUC({lab}) 95% CI:", np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5]).round(4))
print("AUC within each regime (cs / irs / new):")
for r, g in test.groupby("regime"):

          round(roc_auc_score(g.default_flag, g.p_new), 4))
tr3, te3 = train[train.regime == "R3"], test[test.regime == "R3"]
m_r3 = smf.logit(f"default_flag ~ {CS} + {LI} + age_lt25 + age_ge67 + existing_customer", tr3).fit(disp=0, maxiter=200)
print("R3-only fit, R3 holdout AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(te3.default_flag, m_r3.predict(te3)), 4))
print("calibration by regime (new model):")
print(test.groupby("regime")[["p_new", "default_flag"]].mean().round(4))
test["p_new_dec"] = pd.qcut(test.p_new, 10, labels=False)
print(test.groupby("p_new_dec")[["p_new", "default_flag"]].mean().round(4).T)
# business view: among the riskiest 10% / 20% flagged by each model, what share of defaults & losses captured
for col in ["p_cs", "p_irs", "p_new"]:
    for q in [0.1, 0.2]:
        cut = test[col].quantile(1 - q); fl = test[test[col] >= cut]
        print(col, f"top {int(q*100)}%: captures {fl.default_flag.sum() / test.default_flag.sum():.3f} of defaults, "
              f"{fl[fl.default_flag == 1].profit.sum() / test[test.default_flag == 1].profit.sum():.3f} of losses, default rate {fl.default_flag.mean():.3f}")

Q7. Insight: do counteroffers (downgrades or larger down payments) help or hurt?¶

Question. When the IRS falls in the "Conditional" band, Verizon offers a cheaper device or a larger down payment instead of the plan requested. Does that lower default enough to justify the customers and revenue it costs?

Approach. Verizon's profit is a fixed share of price whatever the down payment, so a counteroffer can only pay off by lowering default. Three tests:

  1. Among accepted counteroffers, regress default on the size of the down-payment increase and on downgrade, controlling for IRS, regime and existing customer.
  2. A regression discontinuity at the Approve/Conditional cut-off. Just below it, applicants get what they asked for; just above, they get a counteroffer. If counteroffers lower risk, default should drop just above the line.
  3. Model whether the counteroffer is accepted, to measure the customers it loses.

Findings.

Effect Evidence
Down-payment increase → default None +0.15 per unit share (p = 0.78)
Downgrade → default None −0.06 (p = 0.18)
Default jump at the Approve/Conditional cut-off None R3: 14.5% just below vs 14.2% just above (±0.1); log-odds jump −0.17 (p = 0.26); not significant in any regime or bandwidth
Downgrade → acceptance −0.55 log-odds (p < 1e-70) R3 acceptance: 65% for down-payment-only offers vs 50% for downgrades
+10 pp down payment → acceptance −0.24 log-odds (p < 1e-15) Acceptance falls from 68% (smallest increases) to 47% (largest)

So counteroffers don't reduce default. They (a) make 35–50% of conditional applicants walk away and (b) shrink revenue on downgraded plans: in R3, accepted downgrades earn $85 on average vs $111 for down-payment-only offers.

Impact (R3: 17,483 conditional applicants in 8 months). Alternative: approve every conditional applicant on the device and terms they asked for. Default probabilities come from a logit on accepted counteroffers (IRS + regime + existing customer), which is valid because the counteroffer terms don't change default. Expected profit per plan = price × (0.25 − 0.60p).

Regime Conditional applicants Turned down offer Expected profit, today Expected profit, requested terms Gain
R1 10,824 4,497 $0.75M $1.46M +$0.71M
R2 10,786 5,273 $0.57M $1.38M +$0.82M
R3 17,483 6,936 $1.10M $2.12M +$1.01M (+8.4% of R3 profit)

The highest predicted default among R3 conditional applicants is 22%, so all of them are profitable at the 41.7% break-even. The result holds even if a down payment did cut losses one-for-one: the average increase is 7.4% of price, which at p ≈ 0.165 saves about 1.2% of price per plan, while each lost customer gives up about 15% of price in expected profit.

Business change. Replace the Conditional band with a straight approval. If Verizon wants a risk lever, use one that doesn't drive customers away, such as autopay or a deposit refunded on completion, and test it first.

section("Q7. COUNTEROFFERS")
cond = df[df.initial_decision == "Conditional"].copy()
cond["accepted"] = (cond.final_status == "Funded_Revised").astype(int)
cond["type"] = np.where(cond.downgrade == 1, "downgrade (+dp)", "down payment only")
print(cond.groupby(["regime", "type"]).agg(n=("age", "size"), accept=("accepted", "mean"), dp_inc=("dp_increase", "mean"),
                                            irs=("internal_risk_score", "mean")).round(3))
fr = cond[cond.accepted == 1]
print(fr.groupby(["regime", "type"]).agg(n=("age", "size"), default=("default_flag", "mean"), profit=("profit", "mean")).round(3))
m_def = smf.logit("default_flag ~ internal_risk_score + C(regime) + downgrade + dp_increase + existing_customer", fr).fit(disp=0)
print("default among accepted counteroffers:\n", m_def.summary2().tables[1].round(4))
m_acc = smf.logit("accepted ~ internal_risk_score + C(regime) + downgrade + dp_increase + existing_customer + log_inc + C(device_requested)", cond).fit(disp=0)
print("acceptance of counteroffer:\n", m_acc.summary2().tables[1].round(4))
print(cond.groupby(pd.qcut(cond.dp_increase, 5)).agg(n=("age", "size"), irs=("internal_risk_score", "mean"),
                                                       accept=("accepted", "mean")).round(3))
# regression discontinuity at the Approve/Conditional threshold: mitigation should lower default just above the cut
rd_rows = []
for r, th in df[df.initial_decision == "Conditional"].groupby("regime").internal_risk_score.min().items():
    for h in [0.1, 0.2]:
        g = f[(f.regime == r) & (f.internal_risk_score.between(th - h, th + h))].copy()
        g["above"] = (g.internal_risk_score >= th).astype(int); g["x"] = g.internal_risk_score - th
        m = smf.logit("default_flag ~ above + x + above:x", g).fit(disp=0)
        rd_rows.append(dict(regime=r, thresh=round(th, 3), bw=h, n=len(g),
                            below=g[g.above == 0].default_flag.mean(), above_=g[g.above == 1].default_flag.mean(),
                            jump_logodds=m.params["above"], p=m.pvalues["above"]))
print(pd.DataFrame(rd_rows).round(4).to_string())

# counterfactual: approve every Conditional applicant on original terms (requested device, base down payment)
price_map = df.groupby("device_final").device_price.mean()   # avg price per tier
cond["price_req"] = cond.device_requested.map(price_map)
# default probability for conditionals: use the observed default rate of accepted counteroffers by regime
# (mitigation does not change default, see logit above), refined by IRS via a logit fit on accepted counteroffers
m_pc = smf.logit("default_flag ~ internal_risk_score + C(regime) + existing_customer", fr).fit(disp=0)
cond["p_hat"] = m_pc.predict(cond)
cond["ev_original"] = cond.price_req * (0.25 - 0.60 * cond.p_hat)
cond["ev_actual"] = np.where(cond.accepted == 1, cond.device_price * (0.25 - 0.60 * cond.p_hat), 0.0)
summ = cond.groupby("regime").agg(n=("age", "size"), declined=("accepted", lambda s: (1 - s).sum()),
                                  p_hat=("p_hat", "mean"), ev_actual=("ev_actual", "sum"),
                                  ev_original=("ev_original", "sum"), realized=("profit", "sum"))
summ["gain"] = summ.ev_original - summ.ev_actual
summ["gain_per_cond_app"] = summ.gain / summ.n
print(summ.round(1))
r3c = cond[cond.regime == "R3"]
print("R3 conditionals: max p_hat", r3c.p_hat.max().round(3), "| share with p_hat<0.4167:", (r3c.p_hat < 5 / 12).mean())

Q8. Topline recommendation (assume today looks like R3)¶

Q8a. Break-even default probability¶

p* = 0.25 / (0.25 + 0.35) = 41.7%.

Every funded plan earns exactly +25% of price if repaid and −35% if it defaults. Expected profit per plan = price × (0.25 − 0.60p), which is zero at p = 5/12 ≈ 0.417. This holds for every device tier, price, down payment and regime.

For comparison, in R3:

R3 funded, IRS decile Default rate Average profit per plan
Safest decile 8.7% $158
9th 13.9% $131
Riskiest funded decile 17.1% $98

Even the riskiest funded decile is less than halfway to break-even. A logistic fit of default on IRS only reaches 41.7% at IRS ≈ 5.5, above the highest score in the data (4.36).

section("Q8. BREAK-EVEN")
print(f.groupby(["regime", "default_flag"]).margin.agg(["min", "max", "mean"]).round(4))
p_star = 0.25 / (0.25 + 0.35)
print("break-even default probability:", round(p_star, 4))
r3f = f[f.regime == "R3"].copy()
r3f["irs_bin"] = pd.qcut(r3f.internal_risk_score, 10)
print(r3f.groupby("irs_bin", observed=True).agg(n=("age", "size"), default=("default_flag", "mean"),
                                                 profit=("profit", "mean"), margin=("margin", "mean")).round(4).to_string())
m3 = smf.logit("default_flag ~ internal_risk_score", r3f).fit(disp=0)
b0, b1 = m3.params
irs_star = (np.log(p_star / (1 - p_star)) - b0) / b1
print("R3 logit default~IRS:", m3.params.round(4).to_dict(), "IRS at break-even:", round(irs_star, 3))
r3d = df[(df.regime == "R3") & (df.initial_decision == "Deny")].copy()
r3d["p_extrap"] = m3.predict(r3d)

Q8b. Recommendation¶

Approve more. Verizon is turning away applicants whose expected default (about 16–25%) is far below the 41.7% it can afford. Do it in three steps, each matched to the strength of the evidence:

  1. Approve conditional applicants on their requested terms (high confidence). They sit inside the funded range, the counteroffer doesn't lower their risk, and their predicted default is at most 22%. Impact: about +$1.0M per 100k applications (Q7).
  2. Move the deny cut-off from 1.50 to about 2.45 on today's scale (moderate confidence). That is R2's 1.92 cut-off after removing the 0.53 score shift. 9,699 of R3's 11,195 denials (87%) fall inside the range R2 funded. Their expected R3 default is 18.1% (max 21%), from R2 outcomes scaled for the shock. A cruder check, the riskiest R2-funded group (15.8%) × the R3 shock (×1.6), gives about 25%. Impact: +$1.10M at the model estimate, +$0.68M if defaults are 1.5× higher, +$0.25M if 2× higher. It only loses money if defaults are 2.3× the estimate.
  3. For the remaining 1,496 denials, whose scores are above anything ever funded, run a randomised test first. For example, approve a random 10% and track 6–12 months of payments. It's the only way to learn about the part of the risk curve never observed (Q3c).

Also:

  • Rank applicants better. Replace the IRS with the Q6 model, or recalibrate it. The IRS gives existing customers a bonus worth 33 credit-score points, yet they default more (9.1% vs 7.2% overall; 14.3% vs 11.6% in the riskiest IRS quintile). It also misses the age steps at 25 and 67. This matters less for approve/deny at a 41.7% break-even, but it matters if volume is capped or prices vary by risk tier.
  • Don't tighten seasonally (Q4d), and judge any future tightening by profit, not the default rate (Q4e).

Overall: steps 1 and 2 add about $2.1M on top of R3's actual $12.0M (+18%) across its 100,280 applications. Funded volume rises from about 82% to about 98% of applicants.

Risks and guardrails.

  • The +25% / −35% profit rule is Verizon's own estimate. It leaves out cost of capital, collections and the lifetime value of an existing account. If the real loss on a default is bigger, p* falls (a −50% loss gives 33%), but it is still above every observed group.
  • If the shock deepens, defaults rise for everyone. Re-estimate default rates and the regime adjustment every quarter, with an automatic stop if new approvals default above about 30%.
  • Before rollout, check the new rules for fairness using the self-reported race, ethnicity and gender fields, which is what they were collected for.

# Regime-adjusted score: remove each regime's average score offset so the same applicant gets the same score
# in every regime. R2 (loosest) funded applicants up to a higher adjusted score than R3 does, so R2 outcomes
# give real (not extrapolated) evidence on part of the R3 denied population.
offset = df.groupby("regime").irs_resid.mean()
print("regime score offsets (vs R1):", offset.round(3).to_dict())
df["s_adj"] = df.internal_risk_score - df.regime.map(offset)
f["s_adj"] = df.loc[f.index, "s_adj"]
r3d["s_adj"] = df.loc[r3d.index, "s_adj"]
print("max adjusted score among funded, by regime:", f.groupby("regime").s_adj.max().round(3).to_dict())
smax_r2 = f[f.regime == "R2"].s_adj.max()
ins = r3d[r3d.s_adj <= smax_r2]
print(f"R3 denied inside R2 funded support: {len(ins)} of {len(r3d)} ({len(ins)/len(r3d):.3f})")
f["s_band"] = pd.cut(f.s_adj, [-5, -1, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2.2])
sb = f.pivot_table(index="s_band", columns="regime", values="default_flag", aggfunc="mean", observed=True)
sb["n_R2"] = f[f.regime == "R2"].groupby("s_band", observed=True).size()
sb["R3/R2"] = sb.R3 / sb.R2
print(sb.round(3))
m_adj = smf.logit("default_flag ~ s_adj + C(regime)", f).fit(disp=0)
print("logit default ~ s_adj + regime:", m_adj.params.round(4).to_dict())
ins = ins.assign(p_r3=m_adj.predict(ins.assign(regime="R3")))
print("R3 denied, in R2 support: predicted R3 default mean %.3f, 95th pct %.3f, max %.3f" %
      (ins.p_r3.mean(), ins.p_r3.quantile(0.95), ins.p_r3.max()))
r2_top = f[(f.regime == "R2") & (f.s_adj > 1.5)]
print("R2 funded with adjusted score > 1.5 (would be denied in R3): n=%d default=%.3f; x R3/R2 shock 1.6 -> %.3f" %
      (len(r2_top), r2_top.default_flag.mean(), r2_top.default_flag.mean() * 1.6))
avg_price_req = r3d.device_requested.map(df.groupby("device_final").device_price.mean())
for lab, p in [("model", ins.p_r3), ("stress x1.5", ins.p_r3 * 1.5), ("stress x2", ins.p_r3 * 2)]:
    ev = (avg_price_req.loc[ins.index] * (0.25 - 0.60 * p)).sum()
    print(f"EV of approving in-support R3 denials ({lab}): ${ev:,.0f}  (${ev/len(ins):,.0f} each, mean p={p.mean():.3f})")
